headline: Doormat fluke stack the inlets as summer springs build toward the new moon
subhead: Barnegat Bay got too warm for its own good, the fluke bailed for the inlets, and the canyon window out of Cape May might be the best shot of the year.
body_markdown:
Last week the back bays cooked. Barnegat Bay pushed into the upper 70s — I heard 78 and change out toward the causeway — and that snot grass algae bloom that's been choking the flats did what it always does: it ran the fluke right out of the shallow structure and into anything with current and a hard bottom. That's not a bad thing if you know where to look. Manasquan Inlet, Barnegat Inlet, the channel edges up in Raritan Bay off Keansburg and Great Kills Light — that's where the doormats went, and that's where the guys putting fish in the box have been working all week. Meanwhile offshore, the upwelling that's been sharpening the shelf break has opened up a real temperature seam out around Wilmington and Poor Man's — 10 degrees of contrast on the edge, which is about as good as it gets for a canyon trip.

This week the moon's the story. We're building toward new moon on the 11th-13th, which means bigger springs — more water moving through the inlets on both the flood and the drain. That's good news for fluke guys because more current means more bait getting pushed off the flats and stacked in the deeper holes and channel bends where the doormats sit and wait. It's also good news for anybody chasing bait-driven blitzes on the beach, because bigger tides tend to flush peanut bunker and mullet out of the bays right past the jetties. Watch the evening high stand this weekend — with sunset lining up close to the top of the tide Friday into Sunday, that's your window if there's any bass left holding around Sandy Hook or the Highlands bridge structure. I wouldn't call it a sure thing this deep into July with the water this warm, but it's worth a rod in the sand for an hour.

Fluke has been the most honest bite in the zone. Boats drifting the Manasquan Inlet channel on the outgoing, working 20 to 35 feet with 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, have been putting together limits with fish mixed in to 6 and 7 pounds. Same story at Barnegat Inlet — the deeper holes on the bay side of the Route 72 bridge have been holding better grade fish than the open bay has all month. If you can get live spot, that's still the ticket for the bigger models; guys soaking them on a fishfinder rig tight to the channel drop-offs have been separating the doormats from the dinks. Up in Raritan Bay, the fluke bite off Great Kills and along the Old Orchard Shoal channel has been a mixed bag — some days it's a slow pick, some days you get a stretch where three keepers come over the rail in twenty minutes. Pink Gulp Shrimp on a light jig head has been the better call than bucktails in the muddier bay water, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but the water's clean.

Bluefish have been the one bright spot for anybody who likes a fight. Jumbo blues, some pushing double digits, have been working the surf line from Sea Bright down through Long Branch, chasing bunker schools that are still thick along the beach. Metal — Ava jigs, diamond jigs — cast into the wash at first light has been getting bit hard. If you see the bunker balling up and nervous, that's your cue. Don't sleep on chunking bunker off the Sandy Hook rocks either; the blues have been holding tight to structure there on the last of the incoming.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you, have been a ghost. Water's plenty warm enough — that threshold everybody points to has been cleared for over two weeks now — but warm water alone isn't doing it. I've had exactly zero solid weakfish reports out of Raritan Bay or the back bay flats this week. If you want to burn a tide looking for them, work the deeper edges of the flats at last light on a swimming grub, but go in with your expectations in check.

Offshore is where the real headline is sitting. The temperature break out around Wilmington and Poor Man's Canyon is the widest seam we've seen all season, and yellowfin have been showing on that 100-fathom line. Boats running out of Cape May and Atlantic City hit that seam Wednesday and Thursday and connected. If you've got a canyon trip on the books this week, this is the window — that kind of structural setup doesn't sit still for long, and if the seam tightens back up by the weekend I'd expect the bite to slide with it. Closer in, there's been chatter of bluefin working the 20-fathom breaks off the Jersey coast on the overnight squid drift, worth a look on the darker nights before the moon fills back in.

Looking ahead: the new moon springs peaking the 11th through 13th should keep the fluke bite honest in the inlets — bigger current, more bait movement, better drifts. I'd fish the outgoing at Manasquan or Barnegat with bucktails and Gulp, and if I had a boat capable of the run, I'd be looking hard at that Wilmington/Poor Man's seam before it closes up. Bonito and Spanish mackerel have started showing up the coast at the eastern Long Island inlets — if that pattern keeps sliding south the way it usually does, Manasquan and Shark River could see the first fish any day now. Nothing's shown here yet, but I'd have a small metal rod rigged and ready just in case.
